summary: Defines, with a companion document, an inter-autonomous system routing protocol for the Internet. This is version 3 of BGP. It was on the standards track and is now historic.

plainLanguage.summary: Different networks tell each other how to reach places. This is an early version of those rules.

questions: what are the bgp message types
subtitle: The third version of BGP, the protocol networks use to tell each other which destinations they can reach.

tldr.problem: Separate administrative networks (autonomous systems) need a way to exchange reachability information, including the full path of autonomous systems that traffic must cross, so that routing loops can be pruned and policies enforced.
tldr.mechanism: BGP speakers open a TCP connection on port 179, send their whole routing table once, and then send only incremental UPDATE messages. KEEPALIVE messages show the peer is alive, and NOTIFICATION messages report errors and close the connection.
tldr.outcome: This is BGP version 3, which obsoletes RFC 1163. The metadata marks it as Historic.

facts.label: Suggested timers
facts.value: ConnectRetry 120 s, Holdtime 90 s, KeepAlive 30 s

today: RFC 1267 is marked Historic. It obsoletes RFC 1163, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes it. Its Security Considerations section says only that security issues are not discussed in the memo.

sections.title: What BGP Does
sections.content:
The Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) is an inter-Autonomous System routing protocol, built on experience with EGP. A BGP speaker's main job is to exchange network reachability information with other BGP systems, including the full path of Autonomous Systems (ASs) that traffic must go through. That is enough to build a graph of AS connectivity from which routing loops can be pruned and some AS-level policies enforced.

BGP follows a hop-by-hop paradigm: an AS advertises to its neighbors only those routes that it uses itself. So BGP can support any policy that fits hop-by-hop routing, but not policies that need something like source routing.

BGP runs over a reliable transport, so it needs no update fragmentation, retransmission, acknowledgement or sequencing. It uses TCP, on port 179. The companion document, RFC 1268, covers how BGP is applied in the Internet (RFC 1268).
sections.plainLanguage: Each network is like a neighborhood that only tells its neighbors about roads it uses itself. Together they can learn the whole map and avoid going in circles.

sections.title: How a Session Works
sections.content:
Two systems form a transport connection, exchange messages to open and confirm it, and then send the entire BGP routing table. After that, only incremental updates are sent. BGP does not refresh the whole table periodically, so a speaker must keep the current routing tables of all its peers for as long as the connection lasts.

KEEPALIVE messages are sent regularly to show the connection is alive, and NOTIFICATION messages are sent when something goes wrong. After an error, a notification is sent and the connection is closed.

Connections between speakers in different ASs are external links, and those within one AS are internal links. A speaker decides which it is by comparing the AS number in the peer's OPEN message with its own. For an AS that provides transit, the speakers within it keep direct BGP connections to each other so they share a consistent view of outside routes.
sections.plainLanguage: Two routers shake hands, swap their whole address book once, and after that only tell each other what has changed. They send a quick hello every so often to show they are still there.

sections.title: The Four Message Types
sections.content:
Every message starts with a fixed 19-octet header: a 16-octet Marker, a 2-octet Length and a 1-octet Type. The maximum message size is 4096 octets. The types are 1 OPEN, 2 UPDATE, 3 NOTIFICATION and 4 KEEPALIVE. The Marker is all ones for OPEN messages and for connections with Authentication Code zero, and can otherwise be used for authentication or to detect lost synchronization.

OPEN is the first message each side sends. It carries the version (3), the sender's AS number, a Hold Time, a BGP Identifier (an IP address of the sender), and an Authentication Code with Authentication Data. The minimum length is 29 octets. Only Authentication Code zero is defined, with empty data.

UPDATE carries a Total Path Attributes Length, the path attributes, and then a list of 4-octet network numbers that those attributes describe. Subnets and host addresses are not allowed. The minimum length is 37 octets.

KEEPALIVE is just the 19-octet header, sent often enough that the hold time never expires; one third of the Hold Time is suggested as a reasonable maximum gap. NOTIFICATION holds an error code, a subcode and diagnostic data, with a minimum length of 21 octets, and the connection is closed right after it is sent.
sections.plainLanguage: BGP has four kinds of notes: a hello, a list of routes, a still-here ping, and an error note that ends the chat.

sections.title: Path Attributes
sections.content:
Each UPDATE carries path attributes, each of the form attribute type, attribute length and attribute value. The flags octet has an Optional bit, a Transitive bit, a Partial bit and an Extended Length bit. Attributes are well-known (every implementation must recognize them) or optional, and mandatory or discretionary, or transitive or non-transitive.

The attributes defined in this memo are ORIGIN (1), AS_PATH (2), NEXT_HOP (3), UNREACHABLE (4) and INTER-AS METRIC (5). ORIGIN says whether the networks were learned from an IGP, EGP or some other way. AS_PATH lists the ASs the traffic must cross, using 2 octets per AS. NEXT_HOP gives the IP address of the border router to use as the next hop. UNREACHABLE says that earlier-advertised routes are no longer reachable. INTER-AS METRIC is an optional non-transitive 2-octet value that tells apart multiple exit or entry points to a neighboring AS, where a lower metric is preferred.

An unrecognized optional transitive attribute should be accepted and passed along with the Partial bit set to 1. An unrecognized optional non-transitive attribute is quietly ignored.
sections.plainLanguage: Each route comes with labels, like which cities it passes through and which door to use. Some labels every router must understand, and others it can ignore if it does not know them.

sections.title: The Finite State Machine
sections.content:
BGP behavior is described as a finite state machine with six states: Idle, Connect, Active, OpenSent, OpenConfirm and Established. It starts in Idle and refuses incoming connections. A Start event makes it initialize, start the ConnectRetry timer and try a transport connection, moving to Connect.

Once the transport connection is up, the speaker sends OPEN and goes to OpenSent. After a valid OPEN arrives, it sends KEEPALIVE and goes to OpenConfirm. A KEEPALIVE from the peer moves it to Established, where UPDATE, NOTIFICATION and KEEPALIVE messages flow. Errors, hold timer expiry or an unexpected event send a NOTIFICATION and return the state to Idle. When the Established connection ends, all routes derived from it are deleted.

The memo suggests a ConnectRetry timer of 120 seconds, a Holdtime of 90 seconds and a KeepAlive timer of 30 seconds, all configurable. Version negotiation works by retrying an open with lower versions after an Unsupported Version Number notification. If two speakers connect to each other at once, the connection started by the speaker with the higher BGP Identifier is kept.
sections.plainLanguage: Two routers go through steps like a phone call: dialing, saying hello, confirming, and then talking. If anything goes wrong, they hang up and start again from the beginning.

sections.title: Errors and Route Handling
sections.content:
NOTIFICATION error codes are 1 Message Header Error, 2 OPEN Message Error, 3 UPDATE Message Error, 4 Hold Timer Expired, 5 Finite State Machine Error and 6 Cease. Each has subcodes, for example Bad Message Length, Bad Peer AS, Malformed Attribute List or AS Routing Loop. Checks include a Length below 19 or above 4096, an unrecognized Type, an invalid ORIGIN value and repeated attributes.

When handling UPDATEs, a route whose AS path already contains the local AS can never be treated as better than another route, because using it would cause a routing loop. When a route is passed over an external link, the local AS number is prepended to AS_PATH and NEXT_HOP is updated. Over an internal link, both are passed unchanged, and a route learned over an internal link is not passed to other internal links.

Because routing policies are not exchanged by the protocol, groups of ASs can end up with policies that cannot all be satisfied, which can cause route oscillation. BGP asks a speaker to advertise a route as unreachable before switching to another, so that neighbors can tell a failed route from a merely less preferred one. It does not provide a way to suppress the resulting oscillation.
sections.plainLanguage: If a router hears something wrong, it sends a short error note and hangs up. It also refuses any route that has already passed through its own network, so messages cannot run in circles.
